query: Which Wii-era SDK and middleware libraries have decompilation projects actually matched byte-for-byte against shipped game binaries, and what do the projects' own progress trackers and per-library status files report as matched versus unmatched?

Why does the same library source compile to different bytes depending on the compiler build, optimization flags and SDK revision, and how do decompilation projects use that to tell which exact library version is inside a given game executable?

What happens when a decompilation team claims a function is byte-identical to the original but the compiler build or flags they chose are actually wrong, and how often do such matches turn out to be coincidental?

At what point does matching library functions by signature or hash stop working when the same library is rebuilt with a slightly different compiler build, flags, or linking mode, and what do the resulting misidentifications look like?

What happens when matched library code from one game is dropped into another game that uses a slightly different library revision, and how do projects detect and handle the resulting silent mismatches?

What do the licensing terms, contributor rules and takedown history of Wii decompilation projects say about whether reconstructed Nintendo SDK and middleware source can be shared and reused across projects, and where do they disagree?

What happened to game decompilation or reverse-engineering projects that received takedown notices or legal threats from the rights holder, and what exactly did the notices target: the reconstructed source, the build tooling, or the distributed game assets?
What happens to a project's own codebase and release history when a matched reconstruction it imported is later removed by a takedown, relicensed, or abandoned by its maintainers?

learning: [DERIVED][LOW] The compiler's optimization level changes which transformation passes run, so one source file produces materially different instruction sequences at no optimization, at the first optimization level, and at higher levels. Matching a library inside an executable therefore requires knowing, or searching across, the level it was built with, because a mismatch looks like a different library version. — Capacidad: You can stop assuming that identical source code yields identical machine code, and instead treat the compiler's optimization level as a variable that must be pinned before any binary comparison is trusted. — Evidencia: The GCC manual lists a distinct, enumerated set of passes enabled at each level (for example, the second level adds the inlining of all functions, cross-jumping and tail-call optimization on top of the first), and states that most optimizations are disabled at the zero level. — Ledger: C1 (S1)

[DERIVED][LOW] Which optimizations are active at each level depends on the target and how the compiler was configured, and the inlining size limit is measured in an abstract unit whose meaning may change from one release to another. This means that even with identical flags, two compiler releases can inline or lay out code differently, so byte-level differences can separate toolchain generations and thereby narrow down the library revision. — Capacidad: You can expect that a different build of the same compiler will emit different bytes for the same source, so a fingerprint of the compiler build is itself usable evidence of when and with which toolchain a library was built. — Evidencia: The manual says the enabled set varies by target and configuration, and that the inlining unit's exact meaning might change from one release to another; the link to identifying library versions is my inference, not stated. — Ledger: C2 (S1)

[DERIVED][LOW] When several files are compiled together, the compiler uses information from all of them, and it can inline functions into their callers and then omit the standalone copy entirely, or merge identical constants across compilation units. A library function may thus be absent as a distinct unit in the final executable, so a version check that relies on finding each function intact can miss or misread it. — Capacidad: You can judge that matching a library across a whole program is less reliable than matching it in isolation, since the compiler can merge, inline and discard code using cross-file knowledge. — Evidencia: The manual describes whole-program compilation using information from all files, inlined static functions not being emitted on their own, and constants being merged across units; the implication for version identification is my inference. — Ledger: C3 (S1)

[DERIVED][LOW] Wii and GameCube games share the Dolphin SDK, and matching it once lets every later game reuse those functions, so only game-specific code remains; the Melee project accelerated this way. But CodeWarrior cannot be legally distributed, so projects each document their own toolchain setup and the community is decompiling the compiler itself (mweppc) to escape the dependency. Sharing reconstructed SDK source across projects is technically encouraged, while the build toolchain stays a per-project legal gray zone. — Capacidad: You can plan a reuse strategy around a matched shared SDK layer, accepting that the compiler toolchain it depends on is a separate, legally unresolved dependency. — Evidencia: The wiki describes SDK reuse across games (doldecomp/dolsdk2001, dolsdk2004) and separately states CodeWarrior cannot be distributed legally; the combination is my inference about reuse risk. — Ledger: C4 (S10)

[DERIVED][LOW] Legal analysis in the contents says an open-source label can only license rights the contributor holds, requiring users to supply their own disc does not automatically clear a package that distributes translated game code, and AI generation adds no exception. Projects nonetheless rely on exactly these defenses, publishing code only and asking users to supply game data. Settlements such as re3/reVC and Yuzu are not rulings, so no court has settled whether reconstructed source is shareable. — Capacidad: You can stop assuming that a permissive open-source license or a 'bring your own disc' model makes reconstructed Nintendo code safe to reuse, and instead budget for rights risk at the distribution step. — Evidencia: S9 states the license and own-disc limits and that settlements are not contested rulings, while S6 shows projects relying on code-only publication and user-supplied data. — Ledger: C5 (S6, S9)

[DERIVED][LOW] Projects disagree sharply on AI contributions: N64Recomp prohibits them, RPCS3 permits them with disclosure, and the Wii decomp list shows many projects labeled AI-assisted or AI-generated alongside human-led ones. The GameCube/Wii wiki warns that some projects ban AI contributions, and permitted downstream reuse does not guarantee upstream acceptance. Moving reconstructed code between Wii projects therefore carries a provenance risk that licenses alone do not resolve. — Capacidad: You can treat contributor policy as a project-by-project gate, since code that one project accepts may be barred upstream at another, and check it before pooling work across projects. — Evidencia: S9 contrasts N64Recomp and RPCS3 policies, S10 warns some projects ban AI contributions, and S6 labels Wii projects human-led versus AI-assisted. — Ledger: C6 (S9, S10)

[DERIVED][LOW] In the 2021 Take-Two case over the GTA 3 and Vice City reverse-engineering project (re3/ReVC), the project contained no Rockstar assets and users needed their own game copy, yet Take-Two went after the reconstructed code as 'derivative GTA source code'. It escalated from a GitHub takedown to a California lawsuit naming 14 programmers, partly after three of them filed counter-notifications. Filing a counter-notice can therefore turn a takedown into litigation. — Capacidad: You can stop assuming a reverse-engineered code project is safe because it ships no copyrighted assets, and instead plan for rights holders to go after the reconstructed code itself. — Evidencia: IGN reports a lawsuit naming 14 programmers, filed after a February DMCA takedown, over a project that Take-Two itself was told contained no Rockstar assets, with three counter-notifications cited as bad faith. — Ledger: C7 (S14)

[DERIVED][LOW] On 17 August 2026 Nintendo filed seven DMCA notices at GitHub in one day and removed over 400 repositories. The largest notice covered 311 repositories in the Suyu fork network, because GitHub processes a notice against an entire network once it passes 100 repositories. The theory was anti-circumvention (the emulators cannot work without defeating Nintendo's encryption), not copyright infringement by the code itself. Eden, Citron and Ryujinx escaped because they had moved to self-hosted repositories after February. — Capacidad: You can judge the exposure of a reverse-engineering or emulation project by its legal theory and hosting platform: anti-circumvention claims reach whole fork networks on GitHub, while self-hosting avoids platform takedowns. — Evidencia: Held Games gives specific counts: seven notices, more than 400 repositories, 311 in the Suyu network, a 100-repository network threshold, and the named projects that were not hit. — Ledger: C8 (S13)

[DERIVED][LOW] Nintendo's February 2026 notices gave Switch emulator repositories on GitHub (Citron, Eden, Kenji-X) one day to comply or be disabled, and affected only GitHub-hosted copies. A commentary source says viral decompilation-based mods of games such as GTA 5 are removed within hours, while the decompilation act itself is argued to be protected as fair use. The legal exposure sits in shipping a derivative product, not in the analysis. — Capacidad: You can expect enforcement to be fast and to hit the distributed artifact rather than the underlying technique, so you can plan for a very short response window and for backups. — Evidencia: The Game Rant piece states the one-day deadline and the GitHub-only scope; the TBPN commentary asserts, without verified detail, that mods are taken down within hours. The synthesis is my inference from the two. — Ledger: C9 (S11, S12)
